title: Cleaning the lines
lead: How a draft system is actually cleaned, safely, and how to check that it was.

sections.name: Every 14 days, no matter what
know: Bacteria grow whether a line pours or not.
The cleaner gets stronger the longer you wait.
Older or problem systems may need more.

sections.name: The caustic clean

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Right strength, right heat, long enough.

sections.name: Safety and the log

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Trained people, proper gear, written records.

Chemical into water, never water into caustic.

read.bigIdea: The schedule doesn’t depend on sales.
read.where: The Brewers Association’s **14-day** caustic clean applies however much or little a line pours, because **bacteria keep growing** and their **biofilm** gets harder to remove the longer you wait. Its pre-shift checklist gives **7–14 days** and says to check local rules. Older systems, or ones with flavor problems, may need a tighter schedule.
read.mixup: A slow tap isn’t a clean tap. It may be the dirtiest line on the bar.

read.where: Mix the caustic cleaner (sodium or potassium hydroxide) to at least **2%** for routine cleaning of well-kept lines, **3%** for heavily soiled or old lines or any line that changes a beer’s flavor, and check it with a titration kit. Mix with water at **80–110°F**. Keep it in the line at least **15 minutes** when a pump recirculates it, or **20 minutes** for static or canister cleaning. **Never** use a chlorine cleaner: it damages lines and leaves flavors.
read.mixup: Hotter or stronger isn’t a shortcut for skipping time. The four work together: time, temperature, scrubbing and strength.

video.title: Beer Line Cleaning with the Electric Recirculating Pump | Premier Draft Beer Services

keyPoints.line: rinse until it matches tap water.

read.bigIdea: Move it, rinse it, then descale.
read.where: An electric **pump** recirculating the cleaner is preferred for nearly every system: aim for about **2 gallons a minute**, against the beer’s flow where possible. A pressure canister is a weaker fallback. **Rinse** with fresh water before and after every chemical, until the water out of the line matches a tap-water **pH** reference; never push cleaner out with beer. Every **three months**, add an **acid** clean (phosphoric acid) for beer stone, and **never** let acid and caustic meet.
read.mixup: Acid doesn’t replace the caustic clean. It’s in addition to it, four times a year.

video.title: How To Clean a Draft Beer Faucet Tap: Draft Maintenance

keyPoints.line: cider, root beer, wine stay in a line.

read.bigIdea: Chemical in the line doesn’t clean everything.
read.where: **Faucets** are taken apart and hand-cleaned at **every** line clean, and cleaner is run through every FOB. Every **six months**, **FOBs and couplers** are fully taken apart. Each leg of a split line is cleaned as its own line. Long trunk lines get replaced when the system is **10+ years** old or flavors carry between lines. **Root beer, cider, wine** or flavored beers can **permanently taint** a line and its neighbors, so give them their own.
read.mixup: A new cider on an old beer line won’t just “rinse out”. It can flavor the beer after it for good.

video.title: Beer Draft Line Cleaning - Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)

keyPoints.line: chemical into water, never the reverse.

read.bigIdea: Caustic burns. Treat it that way.
read.where: Only **trained** people clean lines. Wear **splash goggles**, **nitrile, neoprene or butyl** gloves that reach past the wrist (not latex), and chemical-resistant boots. Always add **chemical to water**, never water to concentrated caustic, which can erupt. Keep the **safety data sheet** handy and never leave a clean half-done. Keep a **cleaning log** in the cooler (date, initials, caustic or acid). To check the cleaner’s work, scrape inside a faucet with a straw: a **vinegar or butter** smell means trouble.
read.mixup: A “sonic” line device doesn’t replace chemical cleaning.
